cells.tense: The hands are out and taking in what grew, and the taking is yours.
cells.act: let the inner compass decide the small case
cells.ask: Once this week, let the felt sense of what's fair settle a small case by itself — where an hour goes, or which word you keep — and leave the verdict alone after it lands.
cells.core:
You sense what is owed and what is fair without working it out on paper, and that sense is doing real work. It lets the hands reach and pull what came up under care. They can tell by the weight when something is truly ready, so deciding stays light when it stays light, and small cases run on the part of you that does the knowing.

Keep the count of what is owed, at least the bills that come due in minutes and replies, and settle them as they arrive. Owing somebody a few minutes, a message back, a yes that didn't get delivered: pay it before anyone has to mention it, while it is still the size of a coin. Then what gets done next keeps the same size as the feeling that moved it.
cells.sheetLine: What you can tell is fair, you can act on small.

cells.tense: The count is being taken before the field has finished what it's doing.
cells.act: sit with what the heart already knows
cells.ask: Take ten quiet minutes before deciding anything about this stretch, on purpose. Let the heart's own answer sit beside you. Don't fix it, weigh it, or bring it to anyone. Just stay there with it.
cells.core:
With this much to direct, the reckoning runs past the growing. You tally what the change has made before the change has finished, and the tally comes back wrong and heavy; the gut clenches over a field nobody has harvested yet. Some of that is the waiting itself. Some of it is a season judged by the size of the pile rather than what the rows actually show.

Let the heart arrive before the hands do. Sit with what you already feel about it, without fixing or defending, for as long as it holds. Ten quiet minutes is enough to find that this is feeling, not fact. The right next move tends to show itself from there — not from working harder, from sitting honestly. When it comes, it sits lower in you than the worry did.

cells.tense: The gathering stopped some time before now, and the hands are still out.
cells.act: do the next piece at the speed you can keep for a month, not the speed you can keep for a day
cells.ask: Name one task that still carries weight for you, then do it at a pace you could hold four weeks from now, small enough to manage on a tired day. Once is enough.
cells.core:
The gathering has stopped, and so has the answer to why. Want isn't the part that's missing. What's missing is the second move: settling what you'll do about what draws you, then doing it with your own hands. Without that, the field can't come in, and the day drains out in the gap between.

The way back is a pace, not a push. Name one task that still carries weight for you and do it at a size you could keep four weeks out, not four days. Touch it once, then stop there. The rhythm returns to what your feeling can carry, and movement gets to build without stalling at the edge of each day.
cells.sheetLine: Want is here and no pace is carrying it.

cells.tense: The order of things around here gets set by you, and you'd call it just how things run.
cells.act: put the frame on the table before anyone asks
cells.ask: Next time something with other people gets messy, say the shape of it out loud — this is the order, this is your part, this is the other one — once, plainly, before anybody has to ask.
cells.core:
You set the order of things and speak of it as though the order set itself. The frame people stand in tends to be yours. Nobody corrects it because it holds. What's yours in this is the making — the structure that lets each person find footing — and what's on record is that you were simply handling it.

Say the shape out loud, once, plainly, before anyone asks. Not an argument, not a defence. This is the order, this is your part, this is theirs. Naming the frame in your own voice turns the arrangement back into something you did on purpose, on ground you chose, instead of something that just happened around you.
cells.sheetLine: The order here has your hand on it, and that's yours.

attempts.check: The record names no proof of what the person did before a light went out, and the Too Little cell must stop at showing the hands going through motions without naming who or what caused it. A reader could fairly say that harvesting does not belong to Will at all, that choosing is the opposite of waiting, and the asks must survive that: each is an act that makes a life readable, not a reading of the person. The sentence that serves me more than them is the one that says the work is already in the want; it flatters the draw instead of handing the person something.
